extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and scientists studying inductive logic and the evaluation of evidence/testimony
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from a logic textbook on how to evaluate testimony, improbabilities, coincidences, observation, and description — i.e., the conditions under which reported facts should be accepted, suspended, or rejected and how to distinguish perception from inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total impossibility criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Those which are true of all things whatever, or at least which are totally independent of the varieties of Kinds, namely, the laws of number and extension, to which we may add the law of causation itself, are probably the only ones, an exception to which is absolutely and permanently incredible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assertions contradictory to these most general laws (laws of number, extension, causation) are treated as absolutely and permanently incredible; by contrast, violations of more special or contingent laws should be called impossible only 'in the circumstances of the case' or 'unless some cause had existed which did not exist in the particular case.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension vs improbability rule
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Of no assertion, not in contradiction to some of these very general laws, will more than improbability be asserted by any cautious person... Suspension of judgment is in all other cases the resource of the judicious inquirer.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an assertion is not contradictory to universal laws, treat it at most as improbable and generally suspend judgment unless the testimony, when well sifted, lacks suspicious circumstances and is corroborated by other sources; do not rashly accept or reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sifting testimony for suspicious circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When testimony favors an anomaly, 'the testimony is scarcely ever found to stand that test' of being well sifted; investigators should look for circumstances rendering testimony untrustworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively search for fallacious appearances, epidemic delusions, or implicated interests (religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, passion for the marvelous) that could explain the testimony without the alleged fact; if such circumstances exist, downweight or reject the testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unknown-cause / anomalous-kind caution
rubrics_metrics.description: If an assertion would 'only amount, if admitted, to the existence of an unknown cause or an anomalous Kind' in insufficiently explored circumstances, a cautious person 'will neither admit nor reject the testimony, but will wait for confirmation at other times and from other unconnected sources.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the assertion implies discovery of a new cause or kind rather than contradiction of known universal laws, withhold definite belief until independent confirmation from unconnected sources is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish improbability before and after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The mistake 'in overlooking the distinction between (what may be called) improbability before the fact and improbability after it' — between the improbability of a mere guess and the improbability of an alleged fact being true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject an asserted fact solely because it was unlikely a priori; assess probability in light of the fact's contextual necessity (e.g., one face of a die must occur) and the testimony provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori unlikelihood is not automatic ground for disbelief
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples (die throw, day of death): though the chance against a specific outcome may be great beforehand, this 'is no reason against believing' the outcome when credible testimony asserts it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an event was certain to occur on some particular instance (e.g., someone must die on some day), the prior improbability of a particular label does not justify disbelieving credible testimony that that label occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to overturn general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Events 'contrary to some recognized law of nature, are incredible on any amount of testimony except such as would be sufficient to shake our belief in the law itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accept testimony that contradicts well-established generalizations or laws, require an amount and quality of evidence proportionate to what would be needed to undermine belief in that law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidences as intermediate class needing special evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences are combinations of chances showing 'peculiar and unexpected regularity' and may 'require much stronger evidence to make [them] credible' compared with ordinary events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat coincidences by asking whether the testimony is more likely to arise from false assertion (desire to astonish, love of the marvelous) or from truth; consider motives to falsehood, the witness’ caution, and whether witnesses would be more careful before asserting extraordinary occurrences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-causes test (design vs chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The regular series is not less likely by chance but 'much more likely than the irregular one to be produced by design' (general cause); 'we should rather attribute the effect to a cause which if real would be very likely to produce it, than to a cause which would be very unlikely to produce it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an observed regularity could plausibly arise from a constant/design cause, compare the probability of the event under chance vs under design; prefer the causal explanation that renders the observation more probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing testimony for coincidences by probability of false announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace's and the author's point: to judge a remarkable announcement, estimate 'what is the probability that the given testimony would have been delivered in that instance, supposing the fact which it asserts not to be true.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each instance of claimed coincidence, compute (or qualitatively estimate) the probability that the witness would announce the coincidence falsely (due to error, hallucination, mendacity, or motive); require correspondingly stronger testimony where false-announcement probability is higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for witness error-structure and knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace’s example is critiqued: the credibility of an assertion depends on whether the witness' errors/mendacity operate uniformly across alternatives and whether the witness knew the relative rarity (e.g., 999 black vs 1 white ball).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating testimony, examine whether the witness has more/less scope for particular errors in the asserted form; do not assume uniform distribution of errors—consider how the witness’s knowledge, interests, and the number and distinctness of alternative errors affect reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation vs inference distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The sole condition is, that what is supposed to have been observed shall really have been observed; that it be an observation, not an inference.’ Much that passes for observation contains inference (e.g., hearing a voice vs hearing a sound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating reported observations, separate raw sensations (what was directly perceived) from the inferences superadded (identification, classification). Only accept as direct observation what was genuinely perceived; treat all inferential content according to rules of induction and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions necessarily introduce classification/inference
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘In saying this, I do not solely affirm my sensation; I also class it... It is inherent in a description, to be the statement of a resemblance, or resemblances.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that any description asserts resemblance to known classes and thus contains inferential content; evaluate the reliability of those classificatory inferences (e.g., diagnostic marks, measurement steps, instrument-based deductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurements and instrument-based observations are deductive inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Measurement (e.g., 'it measures ten feet') is 'not an immediate perception, but a conclusion from reasoning' involving mathematical premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat measurements and instrument-based claims as conclusions dependent on instruments, standards, and deductive steps; assess the correctness of those premises and the instrument's reliability rather than treating results as raw sensations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalizations may be more reliable than single observations
rubrics_metrics.description: A general proposition collected from many particulars 'may deserve more complete reliance than it would be safe to repose in any one of the inductive premises' because single observations involve inference errors that aggregate less in many instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing inductive generalizations, consider whether the aggregation of many (possibly fallible) observations reduces chance/error so that the generalization can be more credible than any single reported instance; use this to weigh evidence appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic of observation: discriminate sensations from inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The logic of observation, then, consists solely in a correct discrimination between that, in a result of observation, which has really been perceived, and that which is an inference from the perception.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evidence evaluation, explicitly separate what are the observer’s sensations or states of consciousness from the inferential claims built upon them; apply inductive and evidentiary rules only to the inferential parts and treat sensations as the baseline datum.
